sweep_summary: Four title-keyword items for Paraguayan Guaraní (para1311, catalog: fixed-strict final on StressTyp2/Ayala 1993). Three are Glottolog machine mis-assignments (language code 'computerized assignment from "prosa"/"verso"' on the Glottolog reference pages): Düwel 1978 (Slavic prose rhythm), Caputo & D'Imperio 1995 (Italian prosodic transcription), Funke 1962 (Old English homiletic prose) — not relevant, priority none. The only real item, Clopper & Tonhauser 2013 IJAL (focus prosody; already listed), has no open copy (S2 CLOSED, Unpaywall/OpenAlex not OA, no abstract in any index, UChicago and JSTOR bot-walled, author sites link only the DOI) — paywalled, priority medium. Its 2011 WCCFL precursor (author preprint already held by the project, provenance re-checked against Tonhauser's pubs-by-year page) was read: canonical stress is word-final, but lexical exceptions (óga) and non-stress-attracting suffixes (-ta, -ma) yield penult/antepenult word stress, and the experiment itself used final/penult/antepenult-stressed verbs — refines the strict-final coding toward final-default with morphological conditioning, consistent with the prior check's Estigarribia 2020 and Gregores & Suárez 1967 findings and its reclassify recommendation. Also downloaded Tonhauser 2019 'Prosody and meaning' handbook chapter (scanned, general; not a Guaraní stress source). discovery used author pages, S2/Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Crossref/CORE APIs and Glottolog pages.

new_statements.quote: The canonical position for lexical stress is the final syllable of the word, in which case it is not orthographically marked; if lexical stress occurs in any other position or is associated with a nasal vowel, it is marked by an acute accent or a tilde, respectively (e.g., apyka ‘chair’, óga ‘house’, hatã ‘hard’). Some suffixes attract lexical stress and others do not: the desiderative modal suffix –se ‘DES’, for example, attracts lexical stress (e.g., a-ha-se [...] ‘I want to go’, not *a-há-se), whereas the prospective aspect/modal marker –ta ‘PROSP’ and the perfect aspect marker –ma ‘PERFECT’ do not

new_statements.reading: Final stress is the canonical (default, orthographically unmarked) position; lexically non-final roots exist (óga) and common unstressed suffixes (-ta, -ma) regularly leave word stress on the penult or antepenult, while stress-attracting suffixes (-se) pull it to the end. This is a morphologically conditioned final-default system, not exceptionless word-final stress — the same picture the prior check drew from Estigarribia 2020 (sec. 2.2.2) and Gregores & Suárez 1967 (sec. 5.141), and the same system the catalog codes 'morphological' for Kaiwá, Guajá and Tapirapé. It refines/contradicts the 'fixed-strict final' coding built on the truncated StressTyp2/Ayala 1993 passage.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with, but weaker than, the catalog (final) and the existing Clopper & Tonhauser statement (final default with unstressed suffixes): Restivo confirms that a class of suffixes is unstressed and that stress can be contrastive on particles (tonic vs atonic ramo/rire), which is the morphological conditioning already recorded, but he gives no default placement rule, so he neither confirms nor contradicts 'final'. The editor's 2010 footnotes (n. 70, n. 254) presuppose word-final ('aguda') accent as the living norm.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The 1724 Arte has no section on accent and never states where word stress falls. Its 'Advertencias acerca de la Pronunciación' (pp. 5-7) cover the guttural vowel y, nasality, consonantal j, contracted i, gue/gui, h; 'acento largo/breve' is used only in the old sense tonic/atonic for individual vowels and particles: the epenthetic final -a of consonant-final stems is 'breve' (p. 7), the gerund/supine endings -ma/-pa/-na/-nga/-ka/-ta are 'con acento breve' (p. 75), and ramo is stressed on its last syllable when it means 'now' but 'ambas breves' as the subjunctive marker (pp. 35, 320). Editor Liuzzi's notes add that the modern language keeps such final accents (n. 70, p. 105: 'final acentuado, tal como es aún vigente') and that ãnga 'poor thing' vs ánga 'soul' differ only by 'acentuación, aguda y grave' (n. 254, p. 288).
new_statements.exceptions: Only particle-level facts: unstressed (breve) suffixes -a (epenthetic), gerund -ma/-pa/-na/-nga/-ka/-ta, subjunctive -ramo/-rire; stressed (final-accented) 'ramo' = 'now' and 'rire' = 'after' contrast with their atonic homographs (Liuzzi nn. 21-22, p. 35). No general default position stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Restivo's Arte describes the 18th-century Jesuit-mission Guaraní of the Paraguay reductions (built on Ruiz de Montoya 1640 and Bandini), the direct ancestor of Paraguayan Guaraní; Liuzzi's 2010 footnotes compare it with the modern language ('vigente'). No other variety is described.

sources.note: Word-final stress is the canonical/default position (unmarked in orthography); non-final stress exists lexically (óga 'house') and arises regularly from non-stress-attracting suffixes (-ta PROSP, -ma PERFECT: a-há-ta, a-há-ma vs. stress-attracting -se: a-ha-se). The experiment deliberately built verbs with final, penultimate and antepenultimate stress (root + -ma, root + -ta-ma), i.e. the authors treat non-final word stress as productive. sources.quote: 'PG has lexical stress, typically on the last syllable of a lexical item. However, because many suffixes do not have stress, stress can be on the penult or antepenult of a prosodic word. When a stressed suffix is added, stress shifts to the suffix, and when multiple suffixes have stress, stress shifts to the last stressed suffix (cf. o-karú, o-karú-ta, o-karú-ta-ma, o-karu-pá, o-karu-pa-sé.)' Note 9: 'Guarani roots are to a great extent stress final (the unmarked case), but when an unstressed suffix is attached to it, stress appears on the penultimate syllable of the root [sic].'
